pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 the strategic choice widens to METHODS — mental, jottings, formal written algorithm, calculator — and to measuring tools chosen by the object. The defining act is READING the numbers first and picking a method that fits their features, rather than defaulting to the column algorithm for everything: 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, other digits unchanged), while 345+278 (with regrouping) is where a written method earns its keep. EEF's guidance is explicit that pupils should learn a range of mental, written and calculator methods and make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, self-regulating so they make less but better use of any one method.
bestPractices: Teach pupils to look at the numbers before choosing — sort calculations into 'do in your head', 'jot', 'write out', 'use a calculator' — so method follows the numbers (EEF Rec 4)
Present a range of methods and ask 'when is each appropriate and efficient?', building considered decision-making rather than a single default
Integrate the calculator as a checking tool and teach reasonableness checks, so pupils self-regulate ('less but better') rather than reaching for it or the algorithm reflexively (EEF)
Match measuring tools to the object's size and precision — ruler for a pencil, metre stick/tape for a room — and name why the wrong-scale tool fails
Prize the justification: two methods may both reach 545, so the assessable skill is the reason for the choice, not the answer
keyRepresentations: Measuring tools: ruler, metre stick, tape
commonMisconceptions: Applies the formal written method to everything, even 345+200 or 300+300, because it is the 'proper' way — missing the faster mental route (EEF: not self-regulating)
Attempts a regrouping calculation like 345+278 in the head and drops a carry, misjudging when a written method is needed
Trusts a calculator answer without a reasonableness check
Chooses a measuring tool that doesn't fit the object — a 30 cm ruler for a room — ignoring range and cumulative error

learn.summary: For 7-8 year olds, the target skill is choosing a calculation method (mental, jottings, formal written algorithm, or calculator) and measuring tools by first READING the numbers or the object, rather than defaulting to the column algorithm for everything. 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, tens and ones unchanged), while 345+278 involves regrouping and is where a written method earns its effort. The assessable skill is the justification for the choice, not just the answer — since two methods can both reach 545. Learners also decide which representation fits (for example when an empty number line helps more than base-ten blocks), integrate a calculator as a checking tool with a reasonableness judgement, and match measuring tools to an object's size and precision.

activities.title: Method chooser: route each calculation
feedback: If a learner sets out columns for 345+200, ask what the numbers let them SEE — point to the +200 and that only the hundreds digit changes; invite them to say 545 without writing.

If a learner reaches the right answer by an inefficient method, acknowledge the correct answer but ask 'could you have done that one a faster way? What in the numbers tells you?' — the reason for the choice is the point.

If a learner tries 345+278 in their head and drops the carry, don't reteach the algorithm; ask the meta-question 'is this one to hold in your head, or one to write down?' and let them choose the written method with a reason.
activities.rationale: EEF Recommendation 4 advises teaching a range of mental, written and calculator methods and building considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient; an interactive routing task where the effort of each method is visible is one proposed way to make the strategic payoff felt rather than told. An optional interactive 'bench' can reflect the effort of a slow column build versus an instant mental route to make efficiency concrete.
sourceClaims: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: Work through a stream of mixed calculations (e.g. 345+200, 300+300, 345+278), and for each one first decide out loud which method fits: do it in your head, jot it down, write it out as columns, or use a calculator.
For each, state WHY that method fits before solving — e.g. 'I can see +200, so the tens and ones don't change, so I'll do it in my head.'
Compare the effort: deliberately set out columns for 345+200 and notice how many steps that takes versus saying 545 straight away.
Deliberately choose the written column method for 345+278 and name why (there is regrouping / a carry to track) it is worth the extra effort.

For a given problem, also decide which representation would help most — for example when an empty number line is clearer than base-ten blocks — and say what about the problem makes that representation fit.
Sort a mixed set of calculations into two piles: 'do in your head' and 'worth writing down', and explain what feature of the numbers put each one where it went.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the numbers first and spotting their features (round hundreds vs messy regrouping) lets you pick the method or representation that costs least effort; the column algorithm is worth its effort precisely for the messy cases, not for every calculation.

activities.title: Calculator check: is that sensible?
feedback: If a learner accepts the calculator answer without any check, prompt 'how big should the answer roughly be? Does 623 fit near 630?'
If a learner only trusts the calculator by redoing it exactly, point out that an estimate is faster and still a valid check.
Praise a learner who rounds to check (≈350+280≈630) and concludes 623 is in range, so the calculator's answer is confirmed sensible.
activities.rationale: EEF advises integrating the calculator and self-regulating so pupils make less but better use of it, which requires reasonableness checks rather than reflexive trust. MP5 emphasises recognising a tool's insight and limitations. Here 623 is the correct answer, so the task teaches confirming reasonableness, not rejecting a right result.
sourceClaims: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: A calculator returns 623 for 345+278. Decide whether that answer is sensible WITHOUT redoing the exact calculation.
Estimate instead: 345 is about 350, 278 is about 280, so the total should be around 630 — use that to judge the calculator's answer.

Say aloud a quick reasonableness check for the result: rounding to size (≈630), and the last-digit check (5+8=13, so the ones digit should be 3 — 623 ends in 3). Confirm these checks ratify 623 rather than flag an error.
Practise choosing when a calculator is the sensible tool (awkward numbers, checking) versus when a mental or written method is faster.
activities.intendedInsight: A calculator answer should be checked for reasonableness rather than trusted blindly; estimating the rough size and the expected last digit is a quick way to show an answer is sensible or catch a wrong one, though passing these checks does not prove the answer is exactly right (for example, 633 would also pass both).

activities.title: Fit the measuring tool to the object
feedback: If a learner picks the 30 cm ruler for a room, ask how many times they'd have to move it and what happens to the small errors each time.
If a learner picks a tool correctly, ask them to say the feature of the object (its size) that made that tool fit.
Confirm that there isn't one 'proper' tool — the right choice depends on what is being measured.
activities.rationale: The topic couples arithmetic method choice with tool selection as a single strategic habit of reading the situation before choosing; naming cumulative error from repeated placement makes the limitation concrete, though its size depends on the specific tool and method. MP5 supports making sound decisions about when a tool is helpful and recognising its limitations.
sourceClaims: Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: Decide which tool to use to measure a pencil versus a room: a 30 cm ruler, or a metre stick / tape measure.
Explain why a 30 cm ruler is a poor choice for a room — it needs many placements, and each placement can add a little error that accumulates.
Match a few objects (book, desk, corridor, pencil) to the tool whose range and precision suits them, and name the reason each time.
activities.intendedInsight: The same 'read the job, then choose the tool' habit used for arithmetic applies to measuring: match the tool's range and precision to the object, and recognise that repeated placement of a short ruler can accumulate error.

activities.title: Argue the choice with a method-defaulting partner
feedback: If the learner cannot say why 345+278 is a written-method case, prompt them to point at the regrouping / carry they'd have to track mentally.
If the learner can only say a mental method is 'quicker' when prompted but doesn't choose it spontaneously, give more mixed examples and ask them to route first, solve second.
Reward a clear 'because the numbers...' reason over a correct answer with no explanation.
activities.rationale: A dialogue partner who over-writes everything and springs a regrouping case is one proposed way to pull out the self-regulating rationale EEF says pupils need; justification is the discriminating evidence because both methods reach the same answer. This is one way to elicit the reasoning, not the only way.
sourceClaims: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role tutor) who writes out columns for EVERYTHING, including 345+200, and argue the case for when a mental method is enough.
Respond when the partner springs a regrouping calculation (345+278): decide whether to upgrade to a written method and give your reason.

Answer prompts like: 'Give me a calculation where the column method really IS the best choice, and one where it would be silly', and 'For 345+278, why does writing it down help more than doing it in your head?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a method choice — including when to upgrade to a written method for regrouping — is the self-regulating reasoning the skill is really about.

constraints: The assessable skill is the REASON for the method choice, not the answer: 345+200 and 345+278 can both be checked, but a correct answer reached by an inefficient method does not demonstrate strategic judgement.

Treat a learner who holds 345+278 in their head and drops a carry as a judgement issue about when to deploy a written method, not a gap in the algorithm — do not reteach the algorithm, tune the choice.
623 is the correct answer for 345+278; the reasonableness-check task must confirm it is sensible (≈630, ones digit 3), never lead a learner to reject it.

A scored 'which method?' item can assess recognition of an efficient choice but does not by itself show the self-regulation or reasonableness-checking; use such items to feed into, not replace, a task where the learner routes and justifies.

A static reference chart of 'which method when' is a useful reminder but does not itself let the learner route calculations, feel the efficiency difference, or justify a choice — treat it as a reference alongside, not instead of, the routing task.
Estimation-for-checking (≈350+280≈630) is an approximation used to judge reasonableness, not an exact recalculation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit: 345+200=545 (correct); 345+278=623 (correct). The calculator value 623 used in the checking task is the correct answer, so the 'is it sensible?' task confirms reasonableness (≈630, ones digit 3) rather than hunting a planted error; no activity asks a learner to reject a correct result.

The legacy source rated 3D as 'adding nothing' and a static image/quiz as unable to teach the practice; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been narrowed to scoped affordances/limits (a static chart as a reference; a scored item as recognition-only).
The number-line vs base-ten-blocks representation-choice example from the original evidence was restored into the method-chooser activity.
The measuring-tool cumulative-error point is qualitatively reasonable but its magnitude depends on the specific ruler, object and method; presented qualitatively, not as a quantified absolute.

The formal objective (description) spans multi-digit numbers, decimals and fractions, but all worked examples here are whole-number — consistent with the source's own examples, but decimals/fractions method-choice is not exemplified and would need separate material to cover the full stated scope.
Legacy 'high' confidence and 'verified' source flags were not re-checked in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: Give me a calculation where the column method really IS the best choice, and one where it would be silly.
For 345 + 278, why does writing it down help more than doing it in your head?
A calculator gives 623 for 345 + 278 — how could you tell that's sensible without redoing it exactly?
You're measuring the classroom — why not use your 30 cm ruler? What would you pick, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, the tens and ones unchanged) so the column method is unnecessary work, while 345+278 involves regrouping and is where a written method earns its keep — a judgement driven by the NUMBERS, not a blanket 'always use columns'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the formal written method to everything, even 345+200 or 300+300, because it is the 'proper' way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort a mixed set into 'do in your head' vs 'worth writing down'; ask what the numbers let you SEE (the +200). Build the habit of reading before routing — reteach in place, this is a strategy-selection issue not a gap in the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets out columns for 345+200 and treats a mental method as not allowed or not trustworthy

errorPatterns.pattern: Overreaches mentally on a regrouping calculation — tries 345+278 in the head and drops a carry
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the meta-question 'is this one to hold in your head, or one to write down?'; do NOT reteach the algorithm — tune the judgement of when to deploy it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attempts the hard one mentally and errs at the regroup, having a working written method available but misjudging when to use it

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses a measuring tool that doesn't fit the object — a 30 cm ruler for measuring a room
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match tool to the object's size and precision; name the short ruler's limitation (many placements, accumulating error). Reteach selecting measuring tools.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks a tool whose range or precision doesn't suit the object, ignoring cumulative error from repeated placement

responseLevels.gap: Defaults to one method (usually the column algorithm) for all calculations, or mismatches measuring tools; does not read the numbers to inform the choice.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, reads the numbers and matches the method to their features (mental for +200, written for +278), justifies by efficiency and the numbers' structure, checks a calculator answer for reasonableness, and selects measuring tools by the object's size and precision.
responseLevels.partial: Can say a mental method is 'quicker' for 345+200 when prompted, but does not spontaneously choose it, or cannot articulate what makes 345+278 a written-method case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children work out 345 + 200. One sets out the column method and carries carefully; the other just says '545' straight away. Who chose the better method for THIS calculation, and why? Now what about 345 + 278 — would your advice change?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both methods reach 545, so accuracy is not the tell — the discriminator is whether the child reads the numbers and matches the method to their features (round hundreds → mental; messy regrouping → written). A child who says 'columns is the proper way' for 345+200 reveals no strategic judgement; the second calculation checks they can also justify UPGRADING to a written method.
